title: Almost no one uses AI agents to book their Uber, company says
slides: Uber bet big on AI agents. Did anyone show up?
Very few riders let agents book their trips.
The barrier isn't tech—it's trust in delegation.
Expect slower agent rollout than the hype promised.
Try one low-stakes task and judge for yourself.
thread_text:
1. Uber's Agent Bet Flopped

Almost no riders used AI agents to book trips after Uber rolled out the feature. The tech worked—but people didn't bite.

2. The Delegation Gap

Booking a ride feels personal: pickup spot, timing, safety. Handing that to an agent triggers hesitation even when it's faster.

3. Trust, Not Code

The barrier isn't intelligence—it's willingness to let go. Users worry agents will miss context or make costly mistakes.

4. Slower Rollout Ahead

Expect agent adoption to crawl, not sprint. Hype promised instant delegation; reality shows people ease in gradually.

5. Test It Yourself

Pick one low-stakes task—like ordering coffee—and let an agent do it. Does the convenience outweigh the loss of control?

instagram.caption:
Riders were offered AI agents to book their Uber, and almost no one used them.

The feature worked — people just didn't hand over the trip 🤔

Booking a ride means pickup spot, timing, safety. Letting an agent decide feels like losing control, even when it's faster.

So expect a slower rollout than the hype promised.

If you build or publish content, this is your reality check: adoption lags the demo, and trust decides what ships.

Would you let an agent book your next ride, or is that one tap yours to keep? 🚗
